It sounds like you have no idea how crops are genetically engineered. A organism with a known, desirable trait has it's DNA extracted. The gene that codes for the trait is identified and cut out from the rest of the genome, then that gene is spliced into the crop in different ways until the desired trait is reproduced.

It's not possible to have weird "mystery" traits pop up that didn't come from the extracted gene; the exact same proteins the gene made in the original organism are reproduced in the new crop. There are genetic markers that signal the beginning and end of a protein sequence in every genome, so splicing a gene with these markers on either side into an existing genome will only allow the creation of the desired proteins. Amino acids are encoded by the exact same nucleotide sequences in all plants, animals, and bacteria. A gene that produces a certain protein in one organism will produce only that same protein if successfully spliced into any other creature.

Secondly there's huge fucking incentive for companies not selling plants with an adverse effect, there brand would be destroyed if they were found to be knowingly selling faulty product.

You sound like genetic engineering is a mature science and everything there is to know about genes is already known.

Are you seriously trying to imply that a single gene has one-and-only-one function and that function stays the same no matter where in the genetic chain that gene is located? I'm not even talking about separate species here.

To me it sounds to me like you are the the more poorly informed among us. The way you talk with certainty about science... "It's not possible.." Bollocks. You are not in the least bit the arbiter of what is possible and what is not.

A gene doesn't have a single function, a gene encodes for proteins that have functions. A gene can encode for many proteins, and the expression of these proteins changes based on the conditions of the cell. But a gene doesn't suddenly produce proteins it doesn't encode for when spliced into a new genome.

The big risks of GMO's are the possibilities that the new crops are toxic, and that other organisms will adapt to the new crops in harmful ways. There hasn't been a major case of harmful GMO strains making there way into the food supply in decades, new strains have to be found safe when fed to animals before they're ever greenlit for human consumption. The evolution of "superweeds" is usually pointed at as a terrible consequence of GMO's but they're really only the consequence of using the same few common pesticides everywhere.

Crops in the US were engineered to be resistant to common herbicides, which led to an increased use of those herbicides. This has caused weeds resistant to those herbicides to adapt and spread quickly, choking out farmland which hurts farmers who use those herbicides, regardless of whether or not the crops they grow are modified or not. New herbicides and pesticides will always need to be developed when the old ones grow useless. The sole reason the scale of the current superweed problem is so large is because of the use of the same few strains of GMO seed.

"We don't know all the possibilities" is an empty argument, the data stands on its own. GMO's are at worst no more dangerous than traditional crops, and deliver increases in yields compared to traditional crops. You're falling back on hypotheticals when we're talking about on the most thoroughly researched fields of modern science. Monsanto will pay to have their seeds removed from a farmer's property if they find out. They'll only take legal action if the farmer knowingly uses those seeds to make better crops.

GMO's have been shown to accelerate pesticide use. Here is a study on the subject. Not reduce usage. Unfortunately, the "GMO's use less" argument has been rolled into other, incorrect, and misleading arguments. The true pesticide usage argument revolves around the overall toxicity of the chemical GMO crops are resistant too, in relation to a lot of the other chemicals in use. Companies have misrepresented this fact to make themselves and their products look better. It rarely has to do with the actual quantity, which is actually far higher, now, than it was in the past, and accelerating as usage is leading to greater resistance.

Not to mention that safe to eat doesn't mean "safe." There are many other variables that need to be taken into account and studied, extensively, for every new GMO product that is developed, and released for public use.

Bee Colony Collapse Disorder is a fine example of the impact of chemical resistant GMO solutions being used on a wide scale before adequate research was done, and a GMO food being safe to eat but not safe for the environment. Or for long term agriculture, for that matter.

An example of another relevant discussion is the possibility of genes form other GMO products, like salmon, getting into natural stocks and hurting the survivability of the species.

We need to stop saying that all GMO's are safe. The subject is just too complicated to make such claims.

While there is risk to the ecosystems, this isn't always the case; an increase in nutrient profile will be less invasive than pest resistant crops and so forth.
